title: The Pilot and the Harbor
sum: The speaker turns from the story of Eleazar's death (5:1-6:30) to praise him. Eleazar's reason was a pilot that held the ship of godliness steady through the storm of passions and tortures until it reached the harbor of victory over death; his soul was a besieged city that never opened its gates; his mind was a cliff that broke the waves. He is hailed as a priest who would not defile his holy teeth, a philosopher of a divine life, a new Aaron who stood in the fire for his people, an old man made young by "a reason like Isaac's".

Then the argument resumes. If an old man could look down on torture for godliness, godly reason must rule the passions. To the objection that many people do not rule their passions, the speaker answers that only those who give their whole heart to godliness, who believe that like the patriarchs they "live to God", have the strength; those whose reason is weak are ruled by passion. That is why even boys, as the next chapters will show, could overcome worse tortures.
readings: Read as praise

The chapter is an encomium, a formal speech of praise, of the kind Greek orators gave at funerals and festivals. It piles up images (ship, city, cliff), titles (priest, philosopher, king) and exclamations ("O blessed old age!"). The aim is to make the hearers admire Eleazar and want to be like him.
Read as argument

The praise is evidence for the book's thesis. Eleazar's case proves that godly reason rules the passions (7:16), and the speaker uses it to answer an objection (7:17-23). The hope of life with God (7:19) is the reason that makes such mastery possible, not an extra.

views.O: The Orthodox Church keeps the memory of "the seven holy Maccabee martyrs", "their mother Solomonia and their teacher Eleazar" on 1 August, and its life of the saints calls Eleazar the brothers' teacher, as this book does (9:6). Townshend (1913) noted that the Greek fathers took up the book's praises: Gregory of Nazianzus' oration on the Maccabees is "really a paraphrase of Fourth Maccabees", and Chrysostom applies the image of Eleazar as a sea-cliff to the mother.
views.H: The chapter shows the writer's method. 2 Maccabees praises Eleazar in two sentences (2 Maccabees 6:31); 4 Maccabees spends a chapter, adds the priesthood, Aaron and Isaac, and builds the thesis on him. Historians therefore read the book as a speech built on the story of 2 Maccabees (or its source), not as a separate record of what Eleazar said or suffered.
views.J: For a Jewish hearer the praise is priestly and patriarchal: Eleazar is a son of Aaron (7:12), his reason is Isaac's (7:14), and the faithful live to God like Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (7:19). The model is the Torah's own heroes, not Greek ones. Townshend (1913) found that the book left few traces in later Jewish worship; he could find nothing in the Hanukkah service "that specially recalls Fourth Maccabees".
views.N: Two lines meet the New Testament. "They live to God" (7:19) is close to Jesus' answer to the Sadducees, "to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38), though Jesus argues for the resurrection. And the picture of a death that "seals" and completes a faithful life (7:15) stands beside Revelation's "Stay faithful all the way to death" (Revelation 2:10).
views.G: The language is Greek moral philosophy: the pilot of the soul, the passions as a stormy sea, the four virtues, and the saying that only the wise man is master of the passions (7:23). The Stoics taught that the virtuous person feels no passions; this book keeps the passions and has reason rule them (3:5). Townshend (1913) put it that the author "upholds the Stoic virtues, though not the Stoic" freedom from passion.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant churches do not count 4 Maccabees as Scripture; Townshend (1913) notes it is not in the Vulgate and so is absent from the Roman Bible's Apocrypha "and from our own" (the English). Western churches still honored the Maccabean martyrs, whom Townshend says Augustine and Leo the Great praised in sermons, and read chapters like this one as a witness to Jewish faith before Christ.

deep.b: The speaker chooses two models for Eleazar. The first is Aaron in Numbers 16, who ran with incense into a dying crowd: "He stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was held back" (Numbers 16:48). The second is Isaac, whom 4 Maccabees reads as a willing offering (13:12; 16:20). Both are figures of a life put in harm's way for others: Aaron as a priest standing in the fire of God's anger, Isaac as the son laid on the altar. Together they frame what Eleazar asked for in his last prayer, that God be merciful to the nation and take his soul as a life in exchange for them (6:28-29).

deep.title: Why Aaron? (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. Of all Aaron's deeds the speaker picks the one where Aaron "made atonement for the people" (Numbers 16:47) by putting himself between the plague and the living. That choice may be deliberate: it prepares the hearers to hear Eleazar's death, and then the brothers', as an atoning act for Israel, the claim the book makes outright at 6:28-29 and 17:21-22. If so, 7:11-12 is not a decoration but a hinge between Eleazar's prayer and the book's conclusion.

echoes: Numbers 16:41-50; Wisdom of Solomon 18:20-25; Genesis 22:1-19; Luke 20:37-38; Mark 12:26-27; Revelation 2:10; James 3:4; 2 Maccabees 6:18-31

settings.what: Praise of Eleazar, and the argument it proves
settings.to: His hearers, Greek-speaking Jews, addressed as people who know the story
settings.when: Right after the account of Eleazar's death and its first conclusion (5:1-6:35), before the seven brothers
settings.why: To fix Eleazar in the hearers' minds as a model, priest, philosopher and new Aaron, and to use his case as proof that godly reason rules the passions. The objection and answer (7:17-23) tell the hearers that the strength is open to anyone whose reason is given wholly to godliness.
settings.readers: The first readers were Jews who spoke and thought in Greek, living among Gentiles, for whom Greek philosophy was the language of the educated. The chapter tells them that their own law makes them the true philosophers. Where and when they lived is debated; Wikipedia's survey puts the usual range of dates between AD 20 and 130. Whether the speech was first given at a feast is debated too: Ewald and Freudenthal took the book as a sermon for Hanukkah, while others answer that a sermon would be built on scriptural texts, which this book is only loosely (as Wikipedia summarizes the debate); the speaker praises those who died "at this season" (1:10).
views: R. B. Townshend (1913) placed the speaker among the Jews of Alexandria in Egypt. He argued that the book speaks of the temple service as still going on, so it comes before AD 70; that its hearers seem to live in peace, which fits Alexandria before the riots against the Jews under the emperor Gaius Caligula in AD 38-39; and that its style, its Greek philosophy and its free use of the Greek games suit the great Greek city better than Jerusalem. He dated it between 63 BC and AD 38, and guessed that it was written to steel Jews for a coming test like Antiochus's, when they would be asked to honor a deified emperor.

Moses Hadas (as Wikipedia summarizes him) proposed Antioch: a thoroughly Greek-speaking city with a large Jewish minority that honored the martyrs, as the later Christian churches of the Maccabean martyrs there suggest, and a city whose Greek has words that are rare in Alexandrian works such as 3 Maccabees. Hans Freudenthal and Eduard Norden judged that the book's religious outlook does not easily match Alexandrian Jewish thought. Christian tradition placed the martyrs' tomb at Antioch: Jerome, as Erasmus quotes him (in Townshend's introduction), says they were crowned with martyrdom "in Antioch" and remain buried there, and the Orthodox life of the saints says they were tried in Antioch. The book itself names no city.
The first half of the first century AD

David A. deSilva (Introducing the Apocrypha, 2002, as James Rochford summarizes him) judges a date "in the first half of the first century C.E." most likely. The evidence given: two Greek words, thrēskeia "religion" and nomikos "skilled in the law", belong to about the time of Augustus, and Syria, Phoenicia and Cilicia, which the book names together as one governor's province (4:2), were joined into one unit somewhere between AD 19 and 72. Elias Bickerman proposed AD 20-54, and Hadas agreed, suggesting about AD 40 under Caligula (as Wikipedia reports them).
Late first or early second century

André Dupont-Sommer argued for a later date, under the emperor Hadrian (AD 118-135), and Jan Willem van Henten allows a wider range, finding the last decades of the first century plausible (as Wikipedia reports them). Rochford likewise notes that the book could be as late as the Jewish revolt of AD 115-117 or Hadrian's time.

title: The King's Smile
sum: Beaten by an old man, the tyrant orders young Hebrews brought in. Seven handsome brothers and their aged mother stand before him. He smiles, admires them, and makes them an offer: give up the ancestral law, take part in Greek life, and receive high office as his friends; refuse, and die by torture. To press the point, his guards lay out the instruments: wheels, joint-wrenchers, racks, catapults, kettles, griddles, thumbscrews, iron hands. Be afraid, he says; the Justice you worship will forgive a forced sin.

Before giving the brothers' answer, the speaker writes the speech that cowards would have made: we are young, our mother is old, God will pardon us, the law does not want us dead, why throw away this sweet life? Then he says that the young men said none of it and did not even think it. They were sovereign over their pains. With one voice, as from one soul, they answer the king.
readings: Read as a test of the thesis

The king's offer is an appeal to every passion at once: ambition (office), pleasure (Greek life, youth), fear (the tortures), love (pity for their mother). The cowards' speech lists the excuses. The brothers' silence about all of it is the proof that reason rules.
Read as a mirror for the hearers

The king offers what Greek cities offered ambitious Jews: careers and acceptance if they would live like Greeks (8:7-8). The cowards' speech sounds like what a hearer might say to himself. The speaker puts the temptation into words so that his hearers can recognize it and refuse it.

views.O: Orthodox preachers made the brothers' choice a pattern for Christians: Townshend (1913) reports that Gregory of Nazianzus ends his oration on the Maccabees by telling his flock to "imitate these noble sufferers and do battle bravely with our daily Antiochus".
views.H: 2 Maccabees has no speech of the king to all seven; the king pleads only with the youngest (2 Maccabees 7:24). The long offer, the torture list and the speech of the cowards are 4 Maccabees' own. Townshend (1913) calls such speeches "dramatic inventions", as are most speeches in ancient writing.
views.J: The cowards' arguments are the ones Jewish law later weighed. The Talmud allows almost any commandment to be broken to save a life, on the basis of Leviticus 18:5, but rules that in a time of persecution even a minor commandment must not be broken under threat of death (Bavli Sanhedrin 74a). By that later rule the brothers, facing a royal decree, did what the law required.
views.N: The king's offer of "release" (8:2) is the offer that Hebrews says the faithful refused, "so that they could win a better resurrection" (Hebrews 11:35). Jesus warned his disciples that they would stand before kings and rulers (Matthew 10:18) and must not fear those who kill only the body (Matthew 10:28).
views.G: The speech the brothers did not make is a rhetorical device: the speaker argues the other side in order to defeat it. Its key words are philosophers' words: "necessity" (8:24), and a life "untroubled" (8:26, ataraxia, peace of mind). The brothers reject a calm bought by giving in.
views.W: Western readers have most often drawn a moral lesson from the chapter, the refusal of compromise under pressure. Townshend (1913), writing in Oxford, compares the martyrs' words with those of Latimer and Cranmer at the stake there.

deep.b:
Most ancient writers put speeches into their characters' mouths. The speaker of 4 Maccabees does something rarer: he writes the speech that the brothers would have made if they had been cowards (8:17-26), and then denies they made it (8:27). The excuses are not foolish. Pity for their mother's age (8:20), the thought that God forgives a forced sin (8:22), the claim that the law itself would not demand their death (8:25): each is the kind of thing a thoughtful person might say. That is the point. The brothers are not brave because they cannot see the arguments; they are brave because their reason, trained by the law, sees through them.

Later Jewish law takes one of these excuses seriously. The rabbis ruled that the commandments were given "to provide life" and may be broken to save it, except for idol worship, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed; but "in a time of religious persecution" even a minor commandment must be kept to the death (Bavli Sanhedrin 74a). Antiochus's decree is such a time, and the meal is a public test of loyalty, so the brothers' choice and the later ruling agree.

echoes: 2 Maccabees 7:1-3; 2 Maccabees 7:24; 2 Maccabees 4:10-15; Hebrews 11:35; Leviticus 18:5; Acts 4:32; Acts 28:4

settings.to: The seven brothers, standing around their mother
settings.when: After Eleazar's death, when the brothers are first brought before him
settings.why: To win them with flattery, friendship and office, and to frighten them with the threat of torture, so that they will eat and give up the law. It shows the tyrant's own passion, his pity and anger, at work.
settings.readers: For Greek-speaking Jews the offer was familiar: success in a Greek city often meant living like a Greek. The speech names the price of that success.

settings.to: The brothers, with the instruments of torture set out before them
settings.when: When the guards have laid out the tools
settings.why: To make breaking the law look harmless: their "Justice" will forgive what is forced.

settings.what: The speech the brothers did not make
settings.by: The speaker, imagining the words of cowards
settings.when: Between the king's offer and the brothers' real answer
settings.why: To set out every excuse a frightened person might use and so show what the brothers rejected; it is a speech the speaker says no one gave (8:27).
settings.readers: The excuses are the ones hearers might give themselves under pressure; naming them is meant to take away their power.

title: The First Two Brothers
sum: All seven answer together: Why wait? We are ready to die sooner than break the commandments of our fathers. Your pity, which would save us by breaking the law, is worse than death. Eleazar taught you nothing? Torture us, and you will not harm us; we will win the prizes of virtue, and you will face eternal fire from divine Justice.

The furious king has the oldest whipped, stretched on the wheel and burned until the coals are put out by his blood. He does not groan; he speaks as if the fire were changing him into incorruption, calls his brothers to fight a holy campaign, wishes that the just providence of their fathers may be merciful to the nation and punish the tyrant, and dies. The second is clawed with iron hands, his flesh and scalp stripped away. "How sweet is every kind of death" for godliness, he says, and tells the king that he, the torturer, is the one being tortured.
readings: Read as a contest

The brothers speak the language of the games and of war: prizes (9:8), a post not to be deserted, a campaign (9:23). Each death is a victory, and the loser is the king, whose "proud reason" is beaten by their endurance (9:30).
Read beside 2 Maccabees 7

The first answer repeats 2 Maccabees 7:2 almost word for word, and the second brother is scalped as in 2 Maccabees 7:7. Elsewhere the tortures change, the hope of resurrection drops away, and the brothers claim innocence instead of confessing the nation's sins (compare 2 Maccabees 7:18).

views.O: In the Orthodox calendar these are saints, the first of the seven whose names the church's tradition gives (Abim, Antonius and the rest, in the Orthodox Church in America's life for 1 August). That life adds that their deaths inspired Judas Maccabeus to lead the revolt.
views.H: Historians compare the chapter with 2 Maccabees 7: the joint answer (9:1) is taken from 2 Maccabees 7:2, the tortures are rearranged, and the brothers' speeches carry the book's thesis. Townshend (1913) leaves open whether the extra details come from the writer or from the lost history of Jason of Cyrene that 2 Maccabees summarizes.
views.J: The brothers die for "the commandments of our fathers" (9:1) and the godliness "of our fathers" (9:29), and call themselves "the children of the Hebrews" (9:18). The Talmud's story of the woman and her seven sons, which gives each son a verse of the Torah to die for, keeps the same pride in the commandments (Bavli Gittin 57b).
views.N: "Changing him into incorruption" (9:22) uses words Paul uses for the resurrection body (Philippians 3:21; 1 Corinthians 15:53). The athletic prize (9:8) is the crown of 1 Corinthians 9:25. The cry for vengeance (9:9, 32) stands beside the prayer of the souls under the altar (Revelation 6:10), and in contrast with Jesus' prayer for his killers (Luke 23:34).
views.G: The second brother's claim that virtue's pleasures lighten his pain (9:31) applies the book's opening teaching that pleasure and pain are the roots of the passions (1:20-21). The torturer, ruled by his anger, is the slave; the victim, ruled by reason, is free.
views.W: Western readers often cite Hebrews 11:35 with this chapter, and also note the brothers' threats against the king. Townshend (1913) observed that in 9:9 "There is here no trace of the spirit of the Crucified".

deep.b:
The two books tell the same deaths in the same order and with the same people: seven brothers, their mother and the king. But 4 Maccabees uses them for a different purpose. In 2 Maccabees the brothers' last words carry the hope of resurrection (2 Maccabees 7:9, 11, 14) and the confession that Israel is suffering for its sins (2 Maccabees 7:18, 32-33). In 4 Maccabees the last words prove a thesis: they are speeches about reason, virtue and endurance, the soul that cannot be touched, the prize, and the eternal punishment waiting for the king. The tortures, too, are rearranged (see the note on 9:11), so that each brother faces a different machine from the list in 8:13 and each scene ends with his words.

Each scene follows a pattern: the brother is brought in; he is offered release (except the fifth, who comes forward unasked, 11:1-3); he refuses with a short speech; he is tortured; he speaks again, usually to the king; he dies. The repetition is part of the effect, as in a litany.

echoes: 2 Maccabees 7:1-9; Philippians 3:21; 1 Corinthians 15:53; 1 Corinthians 9:24-25; 1 Corinthians 11:1; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:48; Luke 23:34; Revelation 6:10

settings.when: As soon as he has finished his offer
settings.why: To refuse once for all, before any of them is tortured, and to turn his threats back on him: he will face eternal fire. Speaking together shows that no brother will break.

settings.by: The oldest brother, on the wheel
settings.to: The tyrant (9:15), his guards (9:17-18) and his brothers (9:23-24)
settings.when: During and at the end of his torture
settings.why: To accuse the king, to show the guards that the Hebrews cannot be conquered, and to set his brothers an example: "Imitate me". His last words ask that providence be merciful to the nation and punish the tyrant.

settings.when: As he holds out under the iron hands
settings.why: To show that a greater pleasure masters pain and that the torturer is the one being tortured.
settings.readers: For hearers who might one day face such a choice, the scene promises that endurance has its own joy.

title: A Tongue That Sang Hymns
sum: The third brother is begged by many to taste and be saved. He shouts that he has the same father and mother as the dead, the same upbringing, and will not swear off his brothers. Bring your instruments to my body, he says; my soul you cannot touch. They wrench his joints apart, strip his skin and scalp, and break his spine on the wheel. Dying, he says they suffer for God's training and virtue, and the king will suffer without end.

The fourth brother is warned not to share his brothers' madness. He swears by their blessed death that he will not deny his noble brotherhood. Antiochus orders his tongue cut out. God hears the silent too, the boy answers; you will not cut out our reason's tongue; and God will soon come after the man who cuts out a tongue that sang hymns to God.
readings: Read as a chapter about brotherhood
Both brothers ground their courage in family: same father, same mother, same teachings (10:2), "our noble brotherhood" (10:15). The book will make this love of brothers a long theme (13:19-27).
Read as a chapter about the body and the soul

The third brother says the torturer can reach only his body (10:4); the fourth, that cutting out his tongue cannot silence his reason (10:19). The body is broken piece by piece; the self is untouched.

views.O: The Orthodox life of the saints follows 2 Maccabees for the tortures (the first brother losing his tongue and hands), while this book gives the tongue to the fourth. Gregory of Nazianzus' oration, which Townshend (1913) calls "really a paraphrase of Fourth Maccabees", shows that Orthodox preaching drew on this book as well.
views.H: The fourth brother's tongue scene is the third brother's in 2 Maccabees (2 Maccabees 7:10), moved and enlarged. The torture descriptions are more detailed than in 2 Maccabees; Townshend (1913) remarks that the writer outdoes 2 Maccabees in "dreadful detail".
views.J: The fourth brother's tongue "sang hymns to God" (10:21), the Psalms, and his last appeal is that God hears even the silent (10:18), as he heard Hannah's soundless prayer (1 Samuel 1:13).
views.N: "You will not touch my soul" (10:4) is the conviction of Matthew 10:28, "do not fear the people who kill the body but have no power to kill the soul". The Gospel adds a warning the brothers also give later (13:14-15): fear the one who can destroy both.
views.G: The distinction between body and soul is the Greek one: the soul is the true person and cannot be reached by force. The brothers' reason is the "tongue" that cannot be cut (10:19).
views.W: Western churches do not read this as Scripture; its line that the torturer cannot reach the soul is read beside Jesus' words in Matthew 10:28.

echoes: 2 Maccabees 7:4; 2 Maccabees 7:10; Matthew 10:28; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1; 1 Samuel 1:13; Psalm 35:28

settings.to: The many who beg him to eat
settings.when: When he is brought in after the second brother's death
settings.why: To claim his brothers' faith as his own and to declare that torture can reach only his body.
To name why they suffer, for God's training and virtue, and the king's endless punishment.

settings.what: The fourth brother: warned, and answering
settings.by: The guards (10:13) and the fourth brother (10:14-21)
settings.to: The fourth brother; then the tyrant
settings.when: Before and as his tongue is cut out
settings.why: The guards appeal to self-preservation; the boy answers with an oath, a challenge and a prophecy, and his last words are that God hears the silent and will punish the man who silences praise.

title: Fire That Was Cold
sum: The fifth brother does not wait to be brought: he leaps forward of his own accord, so that the king's crimes against heavenly Justice will grow. What have we done, he asks, but worship the Creator and live by his law? These things deserve honors, not tortures. He is tied to the catapult on his knees, his back bent over the wheel's wedge until he curls like a scorpion. Choking, he thanks the king for the fine favor of a nobler contest.

The sixth, a young lad, says he is younger than his brothers but as old in mind. On the wheel he is burned from below and pierced with red-hot spits. He praises the age in which so many brothers have trained in pain and not been beaten: godly understanding cannot be conquered. Six boys have brought down the tyranny; the fire is cold, the catapults painless, and even the king's guards serve the divine law.
readings: Read as a reversal

Everything in the chapter is turned upside down: the victim volunteers, the torture is a favor, the fire is cold, the tyrant is defeated by boys, and his own guards stand guard for God's law (11:24-27).
Read as an athletic contest

The sixth brother speaks of a "training ground of pain" (11:20): the martyrs are athletes in the gymnasium of suffering, a sharp answer to the Greek gymnasium that Hellenizing Jews had built in Jerusalem (4:20; 2 Maccabees 4:12).

views.O: The Greek fathers loved this chapter's eagerness. Townshend (1913) reports that Gregory of Nazianzus has the youths "boldly demand the torture for themselves", fearing only to miss the crown of martyrdom.
views.H: The fifth and sixth brothers have no tortures named in 2 Maccabees (2 Maccabees 7:15-19); 4 Maccabees supplies the catapult and the spits from its list (8:13). The sixth brother's speech is a compact statement of the thesis (11:21, 25, 27).
views.J: The fifth brother defends the law as the law of "the Creator of all", which teaches virtue (11:5): the same God made the world and gave the Torah, so to keep the Torah is to live by the order of creation. It answers the charge, which a Roman historian later put bluntly, that "Their other customs are twisted and foul" (Histories of Tacitus 5:5).
views.N: The athletic picture runs through the New Testament: "train yourself toward godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7), the crown that never fades (1 Corinthians 9:25), "I have competed in the good contest" (2 Timothy 4:7). The fifth brother's choice to come forward stands in tension with Jesus' counsel to flee from town to town (Matthew 10:23).
views.G: That godly understanding "cannot be conquered" (11:21) is the book's thesis in one line, with "understanding" (epistēmē) in place of "reason". The sixth brother's "noble goodness" (kalokagathia, 11:22) is the old Greek ideal of the gentleman, "beautiful and good", which the book claims for law-keeping boys.
views.W: Western churches honored the martyrs without counting the book as Scripture. Whether a martyr may volunteer, or choose the manner of death, is taken up on the next chapter's page.

deep.b: The fifth brother "leaped forward" (11:1) and "came forward on my own" (11:3); the youngest will throw himself onto the griddles (12:20). The book praises this eagerness: no brother hangs back. Christian preachers loved it; Townshend (1913) notes that Gregory of Nazianzus pictured the youths demanding torture, afraid only to miss the crown. Yet the situation matters. The brothers are already arrested and already commanded to eat; each in turn must refuse. Coming forward does not seek out persecution; it refuses to let fear decide the order. Jesus' advice to flee persecution from town to town (Matthew 10:23) speaks to a different moment, before arrest. The harder question, whether a martyr may choose the moment and manner of death, comes with the youngest brother (see chapter 12).

echoes: 2 Maccabees 7:15-19; 2 Maccabees 4:12; 1 Timothy 4:7-8; 1 Corinthians 9:24-27; Matthew 10:23; Revelation 6:9-11; Genesis 4:10

settings.why: To show that he is not dragged to his death, to add to the king's guilt before heavenly Justice, and to defend the law as the Creator's law that deserves honors, not tortures.

settings.by: The fifth brother, bent on the catapult
settings.why: To mock the king's "favors" (8:6): the torture only lets them show their steadfastness.

settings.when: Before he is tortured (11:14-16) and on the wheel (11:20-27)
settings.why: To show that youth is no weakness when the mind is mature, and to declare the tyranny already defeated by six boys.
settings.readers: The youngest hearers would hear themselves in the lad: being young was no excuse for giving in.

title: The Youngest Brother's Leap
sum: Six are dead; the seventh, youngest of all, is brought in chained. The tyrant pities him in spite of the insults of his brothers, and tries to talk him round: see where your brothers' folly ended; obey, and you will be my Friend and run the kingdom. He sends for the mother, hoping she will save her last son. But she urges him on in Hebrew (the speaker will give her words later). The boy asks to be untied so he can speak to the king.

Free, he runs to the griddles. He calls the king unholy and most ungodly: he received his kingdom from God and kills God's servants; Justice is storing up eternal fire for him; he, a human being, has tortured people made of the same elements as himself. I will not desert my brothers' witness, the boy says. He calls on the God of his fathers to be merciful to his people and to punish the king in this life and after death. Then he throws himself down onto the griddles and dies.
readings: Read as the climax of the seven

The youngest has the longest speech, the king's strongest temptation, and the most dramatic death. His prayer for his people (12:18) gathers up the purpose of all seven deaths, which the speaker will state in 17:21-22.
Read as a chosen death

The boy is not thrown; he throws himself. The book plainly approves, as it approves the mother's leap (17:1). Later Jewish and Christian readers had to decide what to make of a holy death that a person brings on himself.

views.O: In the Orthodox calendar the youngest is one of the seven saints of 1 August. Townshend (1913) reports that John Chrysostom preached that the boy leapt into the braziers "as they had been fountains of cool waters, reckoning them a divine font and baptism": the martyr's death as a baptism.
views.H: In 2 Maccabees the youngest is killed by the king "more cruelly than with the rest" (2 Maccabees 7:39); here he throws himself down. The prayer for the nation (12:18) matches 2 Maccabees 7:37, and Sinaiticus and Venetus even have the same word, "nation". The mother's speech, promised in 12:7, is held back until 16:15-23.
views.J: The Talmud's version has the emperor pity the youngest and offer him the easy way out of picking up a seal (Bavli Gittin 57b), as Antiochus here pities him and offers friendship. The same passage praises captive children who leapt into the sea rather than be forced into sin, so Jewish tradition could honor a chosen death in such a case.
views.N: The youngest's appeal to shared humanity, people "who share your feelings" (12:13), uses the word of Acts 14:15 and James 5:17. His last word about his brothers' "witness" (12:17, martyria) is the word that would become "martyrdom" in the church (see the variant). His prayer that God be merciful to his people stands beside the New Testament's teaching that one death can be for many (Mark 10:45). Whether the sufferings of faithful people can help atone for others, or only Christ's death atones, is the question churches answer differently: see the "Where Christians differ" card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38.
views.G: The boy argues as a philosopher: all humans are made of the same elements (12:13), so cruelty to another is cruelty to one's own nature.
views.W: Augustine, who praised the Maccabean martyrs in sermons (Townshend 1913), is the Western voice consulted for this page. He wrote that no canonical book gives "either divine precept or permission to take away our own life" (City of God 1.20), though he would not judge the holy women honored as martyrs who drowned themselves in persecution, allowing that they may have been "prompted by divine wisdom" (City of God 1.26).

deep.h: A chosen death: how it has been judged
deep.b:
The book tells two chosen deaths with admiration: the youngest brother throws himself onto the griddles (12:20), and the mother throws herself into the fire so that no guard would touch her (17:1). 2 Maccabees has the king kill both (2 Maccabees 7:39, 41), though it praises Razis, who "flung himself off, like a true man, into the throng below" rather than be captured (2 Maccabees 14:43).

In Jewish tradition the Talmud tells the story of the woman and her seven sons right after a story of four hundred boys and girls taken captive "for the purpose of prostitution". The children asked, "If we commit suicide and drown in the sea, will we come to eternal life in the World-to-Come?" The oldest answered from a verse of the Psalms (Psalm 68:22), and they leapt into the sea. The Talmud applies to them, and then to the woman and her sons, a verse of Psalm 44:22, which the Sefaria translation gives as "For Your sake we are killed all the day long" (Bavli Gittin 57b), and it ends the mother's story: "She too in the end went up to the roof, fell, and died" (Bavli Gittin 57b, in the William Davidson translation on Sefaria). There a death chosen to escape forced sin is honored, and the mother, as in 4 Maccabees 17:1, dies by her own act.

In Christian tradition two voices were consulted for this page. John Chrysostom, in a sermon Townshend (1913) summarizes, praised the youngest's leap into the braziers "as they had been fountains of cool waters, reckoning them a divine font and baptism". Augustine held that the commandment "You shall not kill" forbids killing oneself and that no canonical book permits it (City of God 1.20). He would not judge the women honored as martyrs who drowned themselves in persecution: "it may be they were not deceived by human judgment, but prompted by divine wisdom", as Samson was, and he headed the chapter "That in Certain Peculiar Cases the Examples of the Saints are Not to Be Followed" (City of God 1.26).

The text gives the facts each side weighs. The boy is already in chains when he is brought in (12:3), he is untied only at his own request (12:8), and he goes to the griddles after a prayer for his people (12:18-20). Whether that makes the leap a martyr's consent to a death already decreed, or a death he brings on himself of the kind Augustine forbids, the book does not ask; it simply praises him. The topic page Suicide in the Bible gathers the Bible's own cases.

deep.title: The boy on the griddles as an offering (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The griddles (tēgana) were set out to cook the forbidden meat (8:13; compare 2 Maccabees 7:3, 5), and the whole test was whether the brothers would eat from the king's "sacrificial meals". The youngest, after praying that God be merciful (hileōs) to his people, puts himself on the very griddles where the forbidden meat was to be cooked. The scene may be meant as a reversal: instead of eating an unclean offering, the last of the seven makes himself a clean one, as Isaac was "slaughtered" in the book's retelling (13:12) and as Eleazar asked that his blood be a cleansing (6:29). Paul's call to "place your bodies before him as a sacrifice that is alive" (Romans 12:1) is a later Christian echo of the same thought in a different key.

echoes: 2 Maccabees 7:24-41; 2 Maccabees 14:41-46; 1 Maccabees 2:18; Acts 14:15; James 5:17; Mark 10:45; Romans 12:1; Psalm 44:22

settings.what: The king's appeal to the youngest
settings.why: To save face and win one convert: pity, a threat and the offer of a Friend's rank.

settings.when: After his mother has spoken to him in Hebrew
settings.why: To be untied, which the guards take as a promise to give in; it is the opening for his last speech and his leap.

settings.by: The youngest brother, standing by the griddles
settings.to: The tyrant (12:11-15), God (12:18), then the tyrant again (12:19)
settings.when: At the end, just before he throws himself down
settings.why: To charge the king with ingratitude to God and cruelty to his own kind, to promise him eternal fire, to declare that he will not desert his brothers' witness, and to pray for mercy on his people.
settings.readers: For Jewish hearers in a Greek city the boy says what they could not safely say to their rulers: power comes from God, and all people are of one nature. His prayer for the nation tells them that the martyrs' deaths were for them.
